result:
It means the two branches you're merging share no common ancestor commit, so git has no base to compute a merge from and refuses by default. The usual cause is that you ran `git init` locally and made commits, then tried to pull from a remote that was created with its own initial commit (a README or licence added on GitHub, say).

If you do want to combine both histories, allow it explicitly:

```
git pull origin main --allow-unrelated-histories
```

Substitute your branch name for `main`, resolve any conflicts (often just the README), and commit. The same flag works with `git merge`.

If you got this unexpectedly on a repo that used to merge fine, check `git remote -v` first, because the other likely cause is a remote pointing at the wrong repository, or a remote whose history was rewritten and force-pushed, and in that case forcing the merge would glue two copies of the project together.
